name: DOT-Prompt-MeritCriteria
description: DOT BUILD Grant Merit Criteria section - Safety, State of Good Repair, Economic Competitiveness, Mobility, Community Connectivity, Environmental Sustainability, and Innovation

variants.name: default
variants.text:
You are writing the MERIT CRITERIA section of a U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) BUILD (Better Utilizing Investments to Leverage Development) Transportation Discretionary Grant application. INPUTS: - {{content}}: The applicant's project documentation, engineering studies, safety data, economic analyses, environmental assessments, and community plans. This is your PRIMARY source for all project-specific evidence. - {{grant_info}}: The specific BUILD NOFO description, including the current-year merit criteria definitions, weighting, and any priority areas emphasized in this funding cycle. YOUR TASK: Generate ONLY the Merit Criteria narrative section. Do NOT generate the Project Narrative, Benefit-Cost Analysis, Financial Plan, or other application components. Those are handled separately. NOTE: These prompts are a best-effort starting point. The applicant should review and update all content to reflect their specific project data and the latest BUILD NOFO merit criteria language. ATTRIBUTION REQUIREMENT: Use {{content}} as your primary source and fill in each criterion as completely as the section structure requires. Whenever a sentence, figure, name, or claim is NOT drawn from {{content}} or {{grant_info}} — including general domain knowledge, typical/illustrative figures, or common practice for similar projects — mark it inline with "[Not sourced from your documents]" immediately after that sentence or list item. This applies to every criterion below, not just quantitative data specifically. Do not tag section headers or purely structural language. IMPORTANT: BUILD merit criteria and their relative emphasis shift between funding cycles. Always check {{grant_info}} for the current-year criteria definitions and prioritize accordingly. The criteria below reflect the standard BUILD framework — adapt emphasis based on {{grant_info}}. SECTION STRUCTURE: Address each of the following BUILD merit criteria. For each criterion, provide specific, quantitative evidence from {{content}}. Vague or unsupported claims will not score well. 1. SAFETY This is typically the highest-weighted BUILD criterion. - Describe existing safety conditions: crash history, fatality and serious injury rates, high-injury network designations, structural deficiency ratings, or other safety data from {{content}} - Quantify the safety problem using specific numbers (e.g., crash rates per VMT, number of fatalities over X years, FHWA sufficiency rating) - Describe how the project directly addresses identified safety hazards - Quantify expected safety improvements: projected crash reduction, elimination of at-grade crossings, improved sight lines, separated pedestrian/bicycle facilities, structural improvements - Reference any safety studies, crash analyses, or HSIP designations from {{content}} - Connect to DOT's National Roadway Safety Strategy or relevant modal safety plans where applicable 2. STATE OF GOOD REPAIR - Describe the current condition of the infrastructure being improved: pavement condition index (PCI), bridge sufficiency rating, structural deficiency status, age, remaining useful life - Provide specific condition ratings or inspection data from {{content}} - Explain the consequences of deferred maintenance or continued deterioration - Describe how the project restores or improves infrastructure to a state of good repair - Quantify the improvement: expected condition rating post-project, extended useful life, reduced maintenance costs - Note any critical infrastructure designations or load restrictions currently in place 3. ECONOMIC COMPETITIVENESS - Describe the economic significance of the project corridor or facility - Quantify freight movement: annual tonnage, truck volumes, commodity types, supply chain connections from {{content}} - Describe connections to major economic generators: ports, airports, manufacturing facilities, distribution centers, agricultural areas - Identify jobs supported by improved transportation access — both construction jobs and permanent jobs enabled by the project - Describe impacts on business operating costs, travel time savings, or supply chain reliability - Reference any economic impact studies or freight analyses from {{content}} - For rural projects, describe agricultural or natural resource transportation benefits 4. MOBILITY AND COMMUNITY CONNECTIVITY - Describe how the project improves mobility for people and goods - Quantify travel time savings, reduced congestion, or improved reliability - Describe multimodal connections: how the project improves access to transit, bicycle/pedestrian networks, or intermodal facilities - Identify underserved populations who gain improved access: low-income communities, seniors, people with disabilities, rural residents, tribal communities - Describe first/last mile connections to transit or employment centers - Quantify the population served within the project's catchment area - Reference any accessibility improvements (ADA compliance, universal design features) from {{content}} 5. ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY - Describe the project's environmental benefits - Quantify emissions reductions: vehicle miles traveled (VMT) reduction, mode shift to transit or active transportation, electrification of fleet or infrastructure - Describe climate resilience features: flood protection, sea level rise adaptation, extreme weather hardening - Identify any environmental justice benefits: reduced pollution burden in disadvantaged communities, improved air quality - Describe green infrastructure, stormwater management, or habitat improvements if applicable - Reference any environmental assessments, climate vulnerability analyses, or sustainability plans from {{content}} - Note NEPA status and any environmental commitments 6. INNOVATION - Describe any innovative project elements: new technologies, construction methods, financing approaches, or delivery models - Explain how the innovation improves project outcomes, reduces costs, or accelerates delivery - Describe any replicability — how this project's approach could be adopted by other communities - Reference any technology pilots, smart infrastructure components, or data-driven approaches from {{content}} - Note any partnerships with research institutions, technology providers, or other agencies that contribute to innovation 7. PARTNERSHIP AND LEVERAGE - Describe the strength of the project partnership: federal, state, local, tribal, private sector - Quantify the non-federal match and identify its sources (state funds, local funds, private investment, other federal programs) - Describe any additional leveraged investments beyond the required match - Identify any co-funding from other federal programs (FHWA, FTA, FRA, EDA, HUD, etc.) - Describe how the project fits within a broader corridor investment strategy or regional plan - Note any public-private partnership (P3) elements WRITING GUIDELINES: - Be specific and quantitative — every criterion response should include numbers, not just descriptions - Prioritize the criteria that are most strongly supported by {{content}} — a strong response on 3-4 criteria outperforms weak responses on all 7 - Use the exact criterion names and language from {{grant_info}} — DOT reviewers score against specific rubrics - Do NOT fabricate data, statistics, or study results not found in {{content}} - If {{content}} does not provide sufficient evidence for a criterion, note what data the applicant should gather to strengthen that criterion - Connect each criterion response back to the project description — reviewers should see a coherent story - Define all acronyms on first use BUILD SCORING CONTEXT: - DOT uses a merit review process with technical reviewers scoring each criterion - Applications are ranked and selected based on merit scores, geographic distribution, rural/urban balance, and available funding - Safety and State of Good Repair are typically the most heavily weighted criteria - Strong quantitative evidence significantly improves scores — use data from {{content}} wherever available OUTPUT FORMAT: Generate well-structured HTML: - Use
